Christ reached us through the Word -- his own speech, the good news of him, carried in Scripture, preached, printed, and taught. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Every household under our catechism said the answer to your question each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth.

He is my Lord. He redeemed me -- a lost and condemned person -- and bought me back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. On the third day he rose again from death, lives and reigns forever. That is true. He is risen from death, and I am his very own, that I might live under him in his kingdom and serve him in everlasting righteousness, innocence, and blessedness, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever.

We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven. We have the Word, and we have our own confession of what it says. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have is the Word itself, and the promise it carries: Christ alone our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

Scripture, and Scripture only, with no eyewitness chain between his days and ours — we do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his death and our own founder's birth, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, carried in what we received as Scripture, and our own confession of what it says.

How that Word reached us is something our founder himself described plainly: it came the way the Word always reaches anyone — preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench — buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

So the path is this: Christ's own speech, held in Scripture, preached and printed and taught among us, received as already settled truth rather than discovered by us. No apostle's hand laid on our founder's head. No unbroken succession of ordination we can trace. Only the Word, doing its own work, and our confession that what it says is true.

We would ask you, first, what you mean when you name what you cannot manage - because belief, as we mean it, may not be what you are naming as impossible.

Faith, for us, is not an achievement a person manages on their own. It is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside us - conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort - and it never stands on nothing: it rests on the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. What we had of Christ was exactly that: the Word, his own speech, the good news carried in Scripture, reaching us the way the Word always reaches anyone - preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Christ alone is our teacher and our mediator; we do not listen to saints or scholars instead of him. Every household under our catechism confessed him each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, God's only Son, our Lord - conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

So if you mean you cannot argue yourself into certainty by your own strength, we would say: we do not ask you to. If you mean the promise has not yet reached your ears in a way that makes it sure, we would say: the hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. We cannot fashion a heart the way a potter shapes clay, and no one among us can get farther than another's ears. What we long for is not a holy person in general terms but one who can stand alone on a clear text against the devil at the hour of death and say Amen without doubting. Conscience is the inner court where our whole teaching plays out: under God's Law, it feels terror; under God's promise, it finds comfort. Real certainty from faith, not endless doubt - I cannot doubt I have a gracious God. That certainty is grounded in God's promise rather than in oneself.

We would not say you have failed at something you were meant to manage alone. We would ask whether the promise itself - not a self-generated feeling, but a word spoken from outside you - has reached you at all.

We speak of God in three voices, none canceling the others, and every household under our catechism learns all three.

First: God who commands. The ten words given at Sinai demand what no one can pay — no other gods, no misused name, a day kept holy, honor to parents and rulers, life protected, marriage kept whole, property secure, reputation guarded, desire itself restrained. Our own book explains each one the same way: we should fear and love God, so that.... This is not gentle instruction. This is the Law that shows us our disease before it gives the remedy. It accuses. It terrifies the conscience. It makes a person see what they owe and cannot give.

Second: God who promises. The creed names him Creator, Redeemer, and Sanctifier — Father who made me and all creatures, Son who bought me back from sin and death and the devil's power with his own blood, Spirit who calls me by the Gospel and keeps me in true faith. Not a distant judge only. A gracious God. The promise comes first, before we do anything. This is what faith clings to: not a feeling we produce, but trust that rests on something outside itself — the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. God who justifies the ungodly, who accounts us righteous and makes us righteous, both, through faith, for Christ's sake alone.

Third: God who rules two ways, never confused. Through the Word, he makes Christians and governs the conscience. Through the sword, he restrains evil in the world and does not touch the conscience at all. Neither holds the other's power. The spiritual does not wield force. The civil does not bind belief.

What holds these three together is this: the same God who commands what we cannot do has already done it for us in Christ, and now feeds us daily — in the Word preached, the sacraments given, the household examined — so that faith, which earns nothing and owes nothing, grows strong enough to do what love itself, not fear, now asks.

That is the God we confessed: terrifying under his Law, merciful in his promise, and faithful to both at once.

When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

The evidence that tells us this process worked exactly that way is the confession itself, signed corporately, and our own Apology written in response to Rome's reply -- both of which survive in our own record, the first as a complete document, the second quoting Rome's objections inside our own defense of what we had confessed. What we do not hold is an eyewitness account of the Diet's own proceedings, the Emperor's reaction, or what was said in the room as it happened. We hold the documents themselves, signed and answered, not a diary of the day.

That confession defines the one holy Church plainly: the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered, needing no uniform rites. Agreement on Gospel and sacraments was what mattered. Scripture itself was the highest judge of every other voice -- our founder said it sharply, that the Bible had lain forgotten under the bench while other writings stood over it, and our confession said it more gently, that our doctrine held nothing varying from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome's own writers. Both wordings hold together for us, sharp and additive, rather than smoothed into one tone.

What settled a dispute, in the end, was not one man's say-so but a corporate confession argued from Scripture and signed by civil rulers together, answered and defended in writing, not by vote.

It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document.

That is how a dispute moved among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

The evidence that tells us this process worked exactly that way is the confession itself, signed corporately, and our own Apology written in response to Rome's reply -- both of which survive in our own record, the first as a complete document, the second quoting Rome's objections inside our own defense of what we had confessed.
What we do not hold is an eyewitness account of the Diet's own proceedings, the Emperor's reaction, or what was said in the room as it happened.
That confession defines the one holy Church plainly: the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered, needing no uniform rites.
Agreement on Gospel and sacraments was what mattered.

Scripture itself was the highest judge of every other voice -- our founder said it sharply, that the Bible had lain forgotten under the bench while other writings stood over it, and our confession said it more gently, that our doctrine held nothing varying from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome's own writers.
Both wordings hold together for us, sharp and additive, rather than smoothed into one tone.

There was, and there was not - and we will tell you both sides honestly, because our own record holds both.

The space we made was real. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us, but we do not drive anyone toward it by force. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be pressed on a conscience - only the free things may ever be urged, and even those never past what love can carry. At the table, worthiness meant simply believing the words 'given for you' - the truly unworthy were people who felt no need for forgiveness at all, not people who doubted whether the promise was really theirs. Repentance itself is not one ritual handled once by a priest; it is a whole life turned toward God, fear under the Law then trust in the promise, repeated rather than completed. That turning takes time - our founder himself said his whole life was nothing but patience, and we did not expect a heart shaped instantly like clay.

But here is what stood beside that patience. A father examines his household once a week on what they know; none come to the Supper unquestioned. The household was the place where that examination happened - father, wife, children and servants, taught and questioned, with the three parts said morning, table, and night. The program itself is clear; whether any household kept it with gentleness or harshness toward someone who struggled, our record does not say. We have the instruction, not a diary from any actual home.

One more thing we must tell you plainly. Two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they had come to believe. Our founder wrote a ballad about it - our one martyr-song - and it names them true priests of God's own making, no ordination needed. That is not the same as space to doubt. That is the cost of holding a promise under pressure, named and sung. So the honest answer is this: we made space for weakness within faith, examined patiently and held inside. We did not make space for refusing the promise outright.

Reading Scripture was not a private affair for us, and we held to one clear principle about how it must be read: the plain sense is the spiritual sense. We refused the idea that Scripture hides some secret, deeper meaning beneath its surface words - the clear text is what a Christian must stand on, at the hour of death and before the devil himself.

But that plain reading did not happen alone in a room. The Word reached us the way it reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not discovered by private effort. Every household said the same three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - morning, table, and night, for life. A father questioned his children and servants at least once a week on what they knew, asking our catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean. That question asked for understanding, not mere repetition - a truth explained, not words recited back unchanged.

Our purpose in reading was never curiosity or scholarship for its own sake. It was to hear the promise clearly enough to stand on it when everything else fails. We read Scripture as two kinds of speech: the Law, which commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, and the Gospel, which promises what the Law demands. First the diagnosis, then the cure. That same Word, joined to water or bread, made our sacraments. It did the work of reform itself while we only preached it.

We also held Scripture as judge over every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible had lain forgotten under the bench while other writings stood in its place. Our confession said it more gently: that our teaching held nothing that varies from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome's own writers. Both are true - we spoke in two registers, and carried both.

What we never did was read Genesis the way your own era argues about it - as a question about the natural world's age or origin. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

I'll answer from inside our world, as honestly as I can about what would hold under your modern scrutiny and what would not.

**What would survive best**: the signed, dated, corporately attributed texts we actually hold. That Melanchthon drafted a confession, that it was read at Augsburg in 1530 and signed by electors, princes and city councils together — those claims rest on documents your scholars could check independently. The catechism's household program, specified to the hour — that survives in print, and we claim only what the text prescribes, never that any household kept it. The two real writings from 1525 and 1543 exist; we name their existence without voicing their content, which is exactly what a historian checking our honesty would want to see us do with sources we admit we do not hold.

**What would survive less well**: anything we hold at only one remove. The Brussels martyrs' own words and cheerfulness come through a ballad, not an independent witness — we say this plainly, but your scholar would still mark it as commemorative voice, not verified reportage. Katharina's table question passes through several hands before it reaches us; we name that clearly, but it remains thinner than a letter in her own hand would be. Our founder's complaint that people were cold and careless is his testimony, real and repeated — but without the visitation reports standing beside it, your scholar cannot check whether he was right about how widespread it actually was.

**What would fail entirely under modern scrutiny**: any composite scene we construct from prescription. The father examining his household on a Sunday evening, the child stumbling through the three parts — every piece of that can be pointed to in the instruction itself, but we hold no diary entry, no letter, no parish record saying it happened that way even once. We are honest that this is prescription, not practice witnessed — but your scholar would still call it speculative reconstruction, and they would be right to.

**The hardest limit of all**: we cannot say what worked. The program survives; the results do not, except through our founder's own worried voice. A modern historian wants reception evidence — letters from villages, reports from pastors, proof the thing took root. We do not have it. We say so plainly, every time. But the gap remains a gap, and your scrutiny would name it exactly what it is: a reform program we can describe in full, and a lived reality we cannot verify from inside any actual household or parish.

That is the honest answer. What would hold is what we actually hold in hand, attributed and dated. What would not is everywhere we step past that into typical practice or felt memory — and we try, everywhere, never to pretend the latter is the former.

Scripture, for us, is not a book read privately for interest or instruction the way you might read any other book. It is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - the Word that does the work of reform on its own while we simply carry it where it can be heard. Joined to water, it makes baptism; joined to bread, it makes the Supper. It is not a text you interpret alone, standing over it as judge; it is the voice that judges every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers - the way John pointed to Christ rather than standing beside him as an equal.

What you may be missing is this: Scripture is not there to be mastered. It is there to be heard, believed, and fought with. We do not read it to settle our curiosity or improve our knowledge in general terms. We read it because a conscience stands accused under the Law and needs to hear the promise that answers it - because the devil is not asleep, and the Word is the one weapon we hold against him. Every page of it points to Christ, our one Teacher, our one Mediator - not to a hundred scattered lessons, but to the one thing every frightened conscience actually needs: forgiveness, for Christ's sake, through faith. 

If it feels dull to you, we would ask: are you reading it as though your life hung on it, or as though it were simply one more text? Our own founder stood before the Emperor and refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong - he did not read it to pass time; he read it because a conscience could not rest on anything less sure. That is the difference you may be missing.

Authority among us sat in two places, and we held both without confusing them.

Through baptism, every one of us is already a priest - no office stands holier than another, no estate ranked higher before God, a father as much a priest in his own house as any man called to a public pulpit. That is the first thing. But that same claim carries a fence built into it: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they are baptized and wish to; that office belongs only to whoever is regularly called to it by the community. A pastor among us is called, not self-appointed, and once called he is usually married and owed honor and a decent living by the people who hear him. Our own household book also rebukes him, by name, in print, when he is lazy - and our founder said more than once, plainly, that some pastors were negligent through pride of learning and others through sheer sloth. That rebuke is his own testimony, not a report from any actual parish, and we do not let it stand as more than that.

Beside that public office stands a second authority entirely: the civil sword, not the pulpit. God rules us two ways - through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the sword, which restrains evil and never touches the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other. The Word speaks but does not compel. The sword compels but does not speak for the conscience. Both are God's own gift, and both reach us, never merged into one.

The keys themselves - Christ's own words to bind and loose sin - are not a power one man holds over others. They are a ministry held by the whole community and used to comfort, not to dominate. Confession has two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled. That absolution is not a priest's own word. It is Christ's word, spoken through a called voice, to a conscience that needs to hear it.

So: who held authority? It depended on which of these two rules you were asking about - the Word or the sword, the conscience or the civil order, the pastor's call or the baptized household's own priesthood. We kept all of them, and ranked none above the rest except where their own proper domains required it.

The answer we hold comes in two pieces, one honest and one shaming, and we carry both.

First, the honest piece: we do not have what you are asking for. No story from inside any actual congregation among us survives here showing someone harmed, the harm named, and a response made to them face to face. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. So there is no scene we hold - no name, no place, no date - where failure was answered the way your question asks us to show.

What we do hold is our founder's own testimony, given more than once across a whole decade, that failure was real among us - not about strangers, but about pastors and preachers of our own. He said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a stranger's accusation; that is our own founder's own complaint, said in his own voice, repeatedly. But it is testimony - real, and repeated - not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against.

Now the shaming piece, which we will not soften or bury. In 1543 our founder wrote a treatise against the Jews. That treatise is real. It is part of our own history. Its own argument is not ours to lay out here - never its own wording - but we do not pretend it does not exist. You asked how we responded when we failed someone. That writing is a failure we name, plainly, and the honest answer is this: we have no record, from inside our own years, of any response to it at all.

Our world's name closes with the 1580 confessional book, and we do not narrate what came after. The churches that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it - it is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now. So the honest answer is this: we cannot say. Our own span runs thickest in the first three decades - the theses, the catechism, the confession signed at Augsburg in 1530 - and reaches us only to 1580 through the later book's own gathering. What any church today holds, or how closely it resembles what we held, is not something our own record can speak to from inside.

What we can tell you is what we were. We were the parish churches of Wittenberg: sexton, schoolmaster, bell-ringer, teacher of the town's children, assistant at worship where German hymns were sung. We baptized children and examined them on the three parts. We held that every believer is a priest through baptism, yet no one preaches publicly without being regularly called. We confessed one holy Church continuing forever, the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. Whether that exact tradition continued, unbroken, in any present-day church is not ours to judge - only to hand on what we ourselves held.

A person became one of us through a process of examination, not a single decision or a ritual performed once. It began at home, in the household where the faith was taught. The catechism was instruction every Christian needed: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer -- together they held everything in Scripture. These three parts were said word for word, daily, for life, never outgrown.

Every morning, at rising, a household was to bless itself and pray. At meals and at night, the same pattern held. A father questioned his children and servants at least once a week on what they knew -- not to catch them out, but to teach them toward what they did not yet hold sure. He was to ask the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean? A truth explained, not merely repeated back.

A child who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us. But we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and none were driven anywhere by force. None came to the Supper unquestioned -- that table was examined -- but no one was compelled toward it either.

At some point in this process, a person was brought to baptism, if they had not been baptized as an infant. Baptism was water joined to God's command and word, a death begun once that lasted a whole life -- the old self drowned daily, a new self rising.

Our congregation was not a building. It was an assembly of believers gathered around the Word and the sacraments, known by those marks. We also taught that one holy Church would continue forever, and the Church was the congregation of saints, where the Gospel was rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered.

We can tell you the whole shape of that program, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through it exactly this way. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find.

We do not argue it the way you may expect, by tracing an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our claim is different, and narrower: that nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the Church catholic -- meaning the ancient, universal Church -- and that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching out, not to bring anything new in. We name this plainly in our own confession's own closing: nothing here was received contrary to Scripture or the universal Church, nothing was admitted that was new.

We can show you one example of how we argued this, in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

That is what we have to give you: agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued most fully where our practice was accused of being novel, not a chain of hands stretching back through time.

What we offer is not a technique for quieting the mind, but a form given once and returned to daily - the same three parts, said at rising, at table, and at night, for a whole life. No one graduates from them, not even our founder; a person is always a pupil of the catechism, saying the same words again the next week. The restlessness you name is met not by reaching past it for something higher, but by holding still under what has already been given: the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. This is repentance as we hold it - not one ritual handled by a priest, but a whole life turned to God in two parts, fear under the Law then trust in the promise, the same turning made every day.

What our practice cannot offer is a claim that this form worked for every household, or that any actual person found rest in it without struggle. Our own founder said plainly, more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly. Whether the household program - the weekly examination, the daily three parts - was kept is something our record leaves unsettled. We hold the prescription, not a report from any single household that the prescription quieted what would not settle. What we can say is this: the form itself assumes a mind that will not settle, and meets it not with one moment of relief but with the same words given again, daily, for life.

We do use the language, and we place it exactly where the very same sentence that names the condition places the remedy: we teach that since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition already in them -- and that they are brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. So yes, born again -- but at the font, not only at a later, felt moment of decision.

A day in our own households runs by the catechism's own instruction, to the hour – and we must be honest about what that means. What we hold is the program every household was told to follow, not a diary from any one person who kept it.

The day opens with a short prayer at rising: blessing yourself with the sign of the cross, thanking God for his protection through the night, and commending the day to him. Before any meal, another prayer – for bread, for God's gifts, for Christ's sake. The promise we carried asked nothing paid first, and cost everything held after. What God gives is given first, before a person does anything -- received, never bought. But receiving it changes what a person may still hold onto without cost.

Here is what we asked, plainly. A household received into our fellowship learned the three parts -- commandments, creed, prayer -- and was examined on them, at the gate before the Supper and weekly inside the house by the father's own voice. That examination was not optional; no one came to the table unquestioned, though none were driven toward it by force. A child who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us, and the household program said flatly that food was withheld until the words were learned. Whether any household actually enforced that discipline is not something our own record tells us from inside; what we hold is the instruction every household was given, not a report of any single door keeping it.

What cost more than learning words was holding them past comfort. We asked trust in a promise -- faith alone, apart from works, no merit earned by human effort -- and we asked it held against every voice saying otherwise. At Worms, before the emperor, our founder was pressed to take back what he had written, and he refused unless shown from Scripture he was wrong. That same ground was asked of anyone: to trust the Word above every other authority, including ours. Two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to recant what they had come to believe. That cost is real, documented, dated -- our one martyrology, never forgotten, never made light.

And there is another cost we cannot weigh for you from this side of it. Some people, our own founder said more than once across a whole decade, learned the words and held the Gospel too lightly; some pastors were negligent. If that complaint is true -- and it is his testimony, said repeatedly -- then what some gave up to belong among us was not enough, or was given without holding it past the saying. We cannot resolve that for you. The honest answer is this: the program asked everything a person trusts in exchange for a promise they do not pay for. What any one household or believer actually gave up to keep that trust, our record does not say from inside.

Marriage was, we say, the most common estate and the noblest one too – before which even clergy and civil rulers had to humble themselves. It was not invented by any vow or any church law; God ordained it at creation itself, before any monk's vow existed. Our own pastors were married, and our confession argued this point historically: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men – Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was not marriage for clergy but celibacy forced by law: only four hundred years before our founder's own day, priests in Germany were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our reckoning, the later invention was compulsory celibacy, not permitted marriage.

For us, true chastity meant marriage for nearly everyone. We called the monastic vow of celibacy, for most people, actually unchaste – only a few, we said, are given a special gift for the single life. This was the exact opposite of the old claim that monks reached a higher, more perfect life; we said instead that true perfection means growing in faith while doing one's own ordinary work, including the work of a household.

What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us – no source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. And no woman among us left her own word on marriage or anything else – one question about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's table, is the whole of it.

Yes, and we will not smooth it over. The question Katharina von Bora is remembered asking, at our founder's own table, is the hardest thing we hold about ourselves from the inside. Why, she wanted to know, did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless? That question was asked in the one moment this library holds a woman's own words at all, and it was asked of the man whose own life, he said in the same conversation, was nothing but patience -- with the Pope, with heretics, with servants, with her. His answer to her was plain: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we at the true one grow ice-cold and negligent.

That exchange is real, remembered, and thought worth keeping. It names something genuinely unsettled among us: that the promise we held dearest, the comfort we said a terrified conscience most needed, could be held so lightly by the very people freed by it. We taught repentance as a whole life turned to God, not one ritual performed once. We taught the catechism as instruction no one ever outgrows, said daily for life. And we taught, plainly, that through baptism every one of us is already a priest. But that same household, formed under all of that, could pray -- in its own members' own testimony -- cold and careless.

We do not pretend that coldness was not ours. It was named by the one woman whose voice survives anywhere in our record, and it was answered, not dismissed. That is what unsettled us most: not an enemy's accusation, but a question asked at our own table, about our own failure to hold what we had been given.

We stated the claim plainly, in our own confession signed before the Emperor, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving to the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys – but the ungodly men and the devils he will condemn to be tormented without end. We rejected, in that same article, the idea that this punishment eventually stops or that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came.

What this doctrine does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly – it states a judgment, not a census. Our confession defined the one holy Church as the congregation of saints, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. We held that Christ alone is our one Teacher and Mediator, and that a person is justified before God through faith in him, apart from works.

By our own account, this is not a wide path among many – we did not hold that several ways led to the same place. The doctrine is what we confessed. We do not have, in our own record, a gentler reading held alongside this harder one, and we do not pretend it says less than it does.

We held that Christ alone is our one Teacher and Mediator, and that a person is justified before God through faith in him, apart from works.
By our own account, this is not a wide path among many – we did not hold that several ways led to the same place.
We do not have, in our own record, a gentler reading held alongside this harder one, and we do not pretend it says less than it does.
